EDCS-23400495.translation: Chresimion lived 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days. Parents made this for their most devoted son.
EDCS-23400495.summary: This epitaph records the death of a young child, Chresimion, who died at the age of 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days, and was set up by his parents.

EDCS-24700136.translation: The quinquennial duumvirs Lucilius Macer, son of Aulus, and Titus Annaeus Haso, son of Sextus, undertook the construction of the bathhouse by decree of the Senate.
EDCS-24700136.summary: This inscription records the construction of a public bathhouse by two quinquennial duumvirs, Lucilius Macer and Titus Annaeus Haso, in the Roman Republic period.

EDCS-24800013.translation: While our lord Theoderic reigned in Rome.
EDCS-24800013.summary: This inscription commemorates the reign of Theoderic the Great in Rome, likely during the Ostrogothic Kingdom period.

EDCS-25700533.translation: To I. C. Speisander, most glorious and dear, as he was hurrying to the city, Carvilia, his wife, set this up with tears.
EDCS-25700533.summary: This is a funerary epitaph set up by a wife, Carvilia, for her beloved husband, I. C. Speisander, who died while traveling.

EDCS-25700534.translation: Cleopatra set this up with tears for her most sweet daughter Domitilla.
EDCS-25700534.summary: This is a funerary epitaph set up by Cleopatra for her young daughter Domitilla.

EDCS-25700535.summary: This is a very short inscription, likely a personal dedication or ownership mark, potentially from the Roman Republic or early Empire.

EDCS-25700536.translation: To the departed spirits. Lucius Marcus, soldier of the ____th cohort, centurion of Blandus, prefect of the city, gave and dedicated this.
EDCS-25700536.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Lucius Marcus, a soldier, who lived 63 years, with his surviving family members dedicating the monument.

EDCS-25700537.translation: Lucius, son of X, soldier of Rome, with honors, under the amphitheater, he gave and dedicated.
EDCS-25700537.summary: This is a very brief and partially legible inscription, possibly a dedication related to the amphitheater or a soldier's burial.

EDCS-25700538.translation: To Gaius Numuleius Potho, son of Gaius, of the Teretina tribe, veteran of the First Legion Minervia Pia Fidelis, who lived 95 years, 7 months, and 8 days. Lucius Numuleius Merellus, son of Lucius, of the Terentia tribe, from Atina, his patron, erected this according to his will, as is due.
EDCS-25700538.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Gaius Numuleius Potho, a veteran of the Legio I Minervia, erected by his patron according to his will, indicating a considerable lifespan.

EDCS-25700539.translation: Diocletian and Maximian Hercules, at the same time, amplified the Roman Empire; one adopted Galerius in the East, the other Constantius in the West, and made them Caesars.
EDCS-25700539.summary: This inscription is a propagandistic statement from the Roman Empire, likely dating to the late 3rd or early 4th century CE, celebrating the establishment of the Tetrarchy.

EDCS-25700541.translation: To the departed spirits. Lucius Valerius Maximillus, with his own funds, Domician, a most gentle youth, butler, snatched away by an untimely death, lies here. Domician made both the funeral arrangements and the sepulchral honors. (Olympiad) 21.
EDCS-25700541.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Domician, a young butler who died prematurely, with Lucius Valerius Maximillus covering the expenses and honors, possibly dating to the 3rd century CE.

EDCS-25700542.translation: To the departed spirits. Publius Varro Atacinus, very full of wealth, left behind not even the expense of his funeral; he ought to be an example to all, how important it is to be alive if nothing is left for the funeral. Cristilla, his most extravagant wife, placed this for her stingy husband. He lived 48 years, 10 months, and 18 days.
EDCS-25700542.summary: This is a funerary epitaph contrasting the deceased's avarice with his wife's extravagance, intended as a moral lesson, likely from the 2nd or 3rd century CE.

EDCS-25700544.translation: To Laetitia. Gaius Domitius Bassus, son of Gaius, prefect of the soldiers and builders of the 3rd cohort of the Italian Legion.
EDCS-25700544.summary: This is likely a dedication or honorific inscription for Gaius Domitius Bassus, a prefect in a legionary cohort, possibly dating to the Imperial period.

EDCS-25900210.translation: [Cornelius, son of Poplius], [son of Lapir]on, NEA[---]
EDCS-25900210.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription, possibly Greek or bilingual, mentioning a Roman name and a Greek patronymic, likely from a public monument in the eastern Roman Empire.

EDCS-25900217.translation: Under the gymnasiarchs Philion son of Philion, and Onomastos son of Agesippos, scribe Myscos son of Myscos. The people of Rhegion [honored/elected] Gaius Norbanus, son of Gaius.
EDCS-25900217.summary: This is a civic inscription from Rhegion, dating to the period when Philion and Onomastos held the office of gymnasiarch, recording the people's action concerning Gaius Norbanus.

EDCS-26700392.summary: This inscription appears to be a list of quantities, possibly related to funerary urns, with the name Achilles.

EDCS-26700393.summary: This inscription lists quantities of urns and the name Bulos, likely related to funerary contexts.

EDCS-26700402.summary: This is a personal name, likely from a tombstone or other funerary monument, identifying Numerius Hercleidius as the son of Paci.

EDCS-26700420.summary: This inscription provides a personal name, Hercleidius, identifying him as the son of Paci, likely from a funerary context.

EDCS-32900026.summary: This inscription likely refers to Caius Plaetorius Crastus, possibly as the deceased or as a dedicator of a monument.

EDCS-34300259.summary: This fragment suggests Hyginus is dedicating something for himself and at least one other person, likely on a tomb or a religious monument.

EDCS-34300260.translation: To the Spirits of the Underworld. Caliste lived for 7 years. Crysogonus the father made this.
EDCS-34300260.summary: This is a funerary inscription recording the death of Caliste at age 7, dedicated by her father Crysogonus.

EDCS-34300268.translation: [?] to the consul, son of Marcus, son of Marcus
EDCS-34300268.summary: This fragment refers to a consul and includes patronymic information, likely part of a larger honorary or public inscription.

EDCS-34300272.summary: This is a funerary inscription stating that Festus is buried here and was 8 years old.

EDCS-34300273.translation: To the Spirits of the Underworld. For Flavia Berulanen, wife, who lived 26 years. Publius Occius Iulianus, 17 years old, for a well-deserving one.
EDCS-34300273.summary: This funerary inscription is dedicated by Publius Occius Iulianus to his wife Flavia Berulanen, who died at 26, and also records his own age of 17, perhaps indicating he died shortly after or is dedicating it as a young man.

EDCS-34300274.translation: Mario Amandus, freedman and freedwoman of the deified Caesar, and his parents, who lived 17 years, made this for their most devoted son and for themselves.
EDCS-34300274.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for a devoted son named Mario Amandus, set up by his parents.

EDCS-34300275.translation: Sabina, slave of our emperor, may the earth lie lightly upon you. She lived 13 years. Sabinus, her father and master, and Aucta, for their dearest daughter, placed this. Farewell.
EDCS-34300275.summary: This funerary epitaph records the death of Sabina, a slave, and was erected by her father and another individual.

EDCS-34300276.translation: To... Victor, husband, placed this for his deserving wife.
EDCS-34300276.summary: This funerary epitaph records a husband's dedication to his wife.

EDCS-34300278.translation: Quinto Vibiedio Philargyrus, minister of the Lares Augusti, Mercurialis Eusebius and his father made this.
EDCS-34300278.summary: This inscription records the dedication of a monument by Mercurialis Eusebius and his father to Quinto Vibiedio Philargyrus, a minister of the imperial household gods.

EDCS-34300279.translation: Volumnius Pothinus made this for his well-deserving sister, Attia Vitalis.
EDCS-34300279.summary: This is a funerary epitaph by a brother for his sister.

EDCS-34300280.translation: For our most unfortunate daughter, Nome, who lived 20 years and 15 days, [erected by] her mother.
EDCS-34300280.summary: This epitaph records the death of a daughter named Nome, erected by her mother.

EDCS-34300286.translation: M. E. Lucretius, most loving youth, lived 9 years and 1 month. Spurius Campanus for his deserving ward.
EDCS-34300286.summary: This epitaph records the death of a young boy, M. E. Lucretius, and was likely dedicated by his guardian or a relative.

EDCS-34300784.translation: To our lord Flavius Claudius Julianus Augustus.
EDCS-34300784.summary: This is a dedication to the emperor Flavius Claudius Julianus Augustus.

EDCS-34700142.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription mentioning Clodius Priscus.

EDCS-34700143.translation: Of Saturninus, a man of the highest distinction.
EDCS-34700143.summary: This fragmentary inscription refers to Saturninus, a highly distinguished individual.

EDCS-34700145.translation: To the spirits of the departed. Vageilius Uliaisanto lived 7 years and 1 day. His parents made this for him.
EDCS-34700145.summary: A funerary epitaph for a child named Vageilius Uliaisanto, set up by his parents.

EDCS-34700149.translation: He served as a soldier for 12 years. Hum Sabinus made this for his deserving (friend/relative?). Lived to 100 years.
EDCS-34700149.summary: A funerary epitaph possibly for a soldier, commemorating his service and long life.

EDCS-36700003.translation: To the spirits of the departed. Ergastus made this for his well-deserving son Mercurius. He lived 4 years and 17 days.
EDCS-36700003.summary: A funerary epitaph for a child named Mercurius, set up by his father Ergastus.

EDCS-39100023.translation: During the prytany of Nicandros, son of Nicodamus, and the presidency of Sosiopolios, son of Damatrios, of Chios Hippios in the twelfth (month). It was decreed by the Assembly, as by the council and the assembly. Since the Roman general Gnaeus Aufidius, son of Titus, is well-disposed to our city, appearing worthy of his excellence, it has been decreed to crown Gnaeus Aufidius, son of Titus, the Roman general, at the first Athenian games with an olive wreath, and to make him proxenos and benefactor of the demos of the Rhiginians. And his descendants, for the goodwill he continues to have towards the demos of the Rhiginians. And the council, having decorated the assembly hall with two bronze tablets, shall dedicate one in the council-house and send the other to Gnaeus Aufidius.
EDCS-39100023.summary: A decree from the city of Rhiginion honoring the Roman general Gnaeus Aufidius, son of Titus, by crowning him, making him a proxenos and benefactor, and commissioning bronze tablets recording the honor. It dates to the Roman period, likely 1st century BCE or 1st century CE.

EDCS-39100024.translation: The demos (honors) Andron, son of Thrasias Lab-, for his benefactions, to all the gods.
EDCS-39100024.summary: A dedication by the demos (people) of an unspecified city to Andron, son of Thrasias, for his benefactions.

EDCS-39100025.translation: The demos of the Rhiginians (honors) Nicandros, son of Nikonas Teis, to the gods.
EDCS-39100025.summary: A dedication by the demos of Rhiginion to Nicandros, son of Nikonas Teis.

EDCS-39100026.translation: Under the archons Nicandros, son of Leukios, Symmachos, son of Herakleitos, Phylakos, son of Philistion, Kratippos, son of Kratippos, the association of artists and proxenoi of Dionysos (honors) Ainesoun, son of Nikonas Teis.
EDCS-39100026.summary: A dedication by the association of artists and proxenoi of Dionysos during the archonship of several individuals, honoring Ainesoun, son of Nikonas Teis.

EDCS-39100027.translation: Under the archons Aristeas, son of Aristomachos, Amphim [son of] Dionysios, son of Orthos, Erg [son of...], with Kleodamos, son of Myskos, as secretary, the association of athletes (honors) Aristomachos, son of Aristeas Amphim, who served as gymnasiarch.
EDCS-39100027.summary: A dedication by the association of athletes during the archonship of Aristeas and Dionysios, honoring Aristomachos for his service as gymnasiarch.

EDCS-39100028.translation: The chief prytanis and five-year archon from his own funds, Sextus Noumnonius Maturos, son of Sextus; co-prytaneis Quintus Ortorius Balbillus, son of Quintus, Marcus Petronius Pulcher, son of Marcus, Marcus Cornelius Martiallis, son of Marcus; hieroscopes Manius Cornelius Verus, Gaius Antonius; sacrificial priest and sacred trumpeter Gaius Julius Rhiginos; sacred herald Gaius Calpurnius Verus; sacred attendant Quintus Caecilius Rhiginos; treasurer Meliphthongos, son of Maturos; sponsalis (officiant) Natales; capnaugēs Helikon, son of Maturos; magiros Zosimos.
EDCS-39100028.summary: A list of officials, including a chief prytanis, archon, co-prytaneis, hieroscopes, priest, herald, attendant, treasurer, and other functionaries, likely from a Greek city under Roman influence, recorded on a public document.

EDCS-39100029.translation: [Prytanis] and archon from his own funds, Gaius Popillius Julianus, son of Gaius; co-prytaneis Gaius Popillius Frequentinus, son of Gaius Popillius, Titus Vettius Domitianus; seer Gaius Noumnonius Cerealis; sacred herald Gaius Julius Syntrophianos; sponsalis Ktes; capnaugai Bryanthos, Ph[---] Epitunchanos, son of Iulianos.
EDCS-39100029.summary: A list of officials, including a prytanis, archon, co-prytaneis, seer, herald, and other functionaries, likely from a Greek city under Roman influence, recorded on a public document with some restorations.

EDCS-39100033.translation: Timandros Moschionos, in fulfillment of a vow.
EDCS-39100033.summary: This is a vow inscription by Timandros Moschionos, likely a private dedication.

EDCS-39100034.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription that likely refers to a person named Cornelius.

EDCS-39100035.translation: To the Chthonic Gods. Protas lived for 8 years.
EDCS-39100035.summary: This is a dedication to the Chthonic Gods and a record of the lifespan of Protas.

EDCS-39100036.translation: Secundion with his sweetest daughter Philikla and Leonis. If anyone wishes to return, they must render an account in the future.

EDCS-39100040.translation: Here lies Sergius, servant of Christ, who was among the most glorious in memory, of senatorial and ducal rank, who lived 43 years. He was completed in the month of June, the 23rd day, in the 4th indiction. May the reader pray for me through the Lord.

EDCS-39100042.translation: Oiniadas, Eukelados, and Cheimarros dedicated [this] to the goddess.

EDCS-39100043.summary: This is a dedication of an object (implied by 'me') by Xena to Periphanai.

EDCS-39100047.translation: God Tyche gives the house and all other things to Sikainia. Damiorgos: Paragoras. Proxeni: Minkos, Harmoxidamos, Agatharchos, Onatas, Epikorus.

EDCS-39100048.translation: During the gymnasiarchy of Minatus Kriti, Minatus Mariou Kriti, Minatus Mariou, the stoa was reconstructed with public funds.

EDCS-39100049.translation: You will find a spring to the left of Hades' houses, and beside it a white cypress standing. You will not even approach this spring. You will find another spring of Mnemosyne, from which flows cool water. Guards stand before [it]. Speak: 'I am a child of earth and starry heaven, but my lineage is divine. And you yourselves know this: I am drying up with thirst and perishing. So give me quickly cool water flowing from the spring of Mnemosyne, and they themselves will give you to drink from a divine spring, and then you will be led among other heroes.' To die is a terrible thing. Toglos Pas wrote this, enveloping [me] in darkness.
EDCS-39100049.summary: This is a funerary epigram, likely a curse or protective inscription on a tomb, warning visitors away from a specific spring and requesting water for the deceased, attributed to Toglos Pas.

EDCS-39100054.translation: I am sacred to Hera. Kyniskos, son of Hortamos, dedicated me, a tenth of his work.
EDCS-39100054.summary: A religious dedication to the goddess Hera, likely from a rural setting, specifying a tenth of the work as an offering.

EDCS-39100055.translation: Kollyra is vexing the attendants of the goddess concerning the garment she received and does not return, and is using it. And if she knows it, she shall dedicate to the goddess twelvefold with a medimnos of incense, as the city decrees, and not before she dedicates it to the goddess shall she depart from life. Kollyra is vexing the attendants of the goddess concerning the three gold pieces she received from Melita and does not return. She shall dedicate to the goddess twelvefold with a medimnos of incense, as the city decrees, and not before she dedicates it to the goddess shall she depart from life. And if she has intercourse or eats with someone, may I not be innocent or may I come under the same eagle.
EDCS-39100055.summary: A complex curse or legal text detailing a dispute over a garment and gold, with severe penalties for non-compliance, likely from a sanctuary or legal setting.

EDCS-39100056.translation: Superintendent Aristarchos, son of Herakleidas; month of Apellaios. The city and the overseers [erected] the tripod for Philonymos, son of Zopyris; the spice box for Apollonios, son of Herakles; the shield for Dazimos, son of Pyrros; the trivet for Philotas, son of Histieus; the epistyle for Herakleidas, son of Zopyros, to Dionysos. They inscribed them, the overseers who were chosen for the sacred lands of Dionysos: Philonymos, son of Zopyris; Apollonios, son of Herakles; Dazimos, son of Pyrros; Philotas, son of Histieus; Herakleidas, son of Zopyros, according to what they marked out, finished, measured, and divided. We measured the boundaries of the sacred and private lands, as the Herakleians decreed in the assembly in Aliai, beginning from the boundary stone beyond Pandosia, which divides the sacred lands and the private land, to the boundary stone marking the horizon, of both the lands of Dionysos and the private land of the Koniates. We demarcated four parts. The first part, from the boundary stone near the heroön, extending one hundred feet in width towards the thirty-foot [path?] running through the sacred lands, and in length from the upper boundary to the river Akiris. And they were measured in this part: cultivated land, one hundred and twenty schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, six hundred and forty-six and a half schoinoi. The second part, in width from the thirty-foot [path?] to the first boundary stone, and in length from the upper boundary to the river. And they were measured in this part: cultivated land, two hundred and seventy-three schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, five hundred schoinoi. The third part, in width from the first boundary stone, which runs near the thirty-foot [path?], to the second boundary stone from the thirty-foot [path?], and in length from the upper boundary to the river. And they were measured in this part: cultivated land, three hundred and twelve and a half schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, five hundred and thirty-seven and a half schoinoi. The fourth part, in width from the second boundary stone from the thirty-foot [path?] to the horizon boundary stone, of both the sacred and the private land, and in length from the upper boundary to the river. And they were measured in this part: cultivated land, three hundred and eight and a half schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, five hundred and forty-one and a half schoinoi. The total of all cultivated land, one thousand one hundred and ninety-five schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, two thousand two hundred and twenty-five schoinoi. The island added to the uncultivated land, we measured from this land. Lost: cultivated land, three hundred and three and a half schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, four hundred and thirty-five schoinoi. In the first part, near the heroön: cultivated land, seventy-six schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, one hundred and eighty-five schoinoi. In the fourth part, near the Fintias: cultivated land, two hundred and twenty-seven and a half schoinoi; scrub, uncultivated land, and woodland, two hundred and fifty schoinoi. Total of all land dedicated to Dionysos, seven hundred and thirty-eight and a half schoinoi. We dedicated this land, having obtained judgments in thirty lawsuits against those who made the sacred land private. This land was rented out for life, for as much as we dedicated, at thirty medimnoi per year. The total land for Dionysos is four hundred and ten medimnoi per year. We also set up boundary stones. On the upper side, one on the boundary stone near Pandosia, near the heroön, marking the horizon, of both the sacred and private land, separating it from the upper boundary, so that it would not be encroached upon, as were the previous boundary stones. Another on the boundary stone near the Fintias, along the canal and the ditch, similarly separating it into private land. And other boundary stones between these, set up on the road through the gorge, leading past the woodland, the pillars on the sacred land, and the boundary stones on the private land, leaving a hundred-foot boundary. We also set up intermediate boundary stones: two on the road leading from the city and from Pandosia through the sacred lands, and two on the high ridges. All these, in alignment with each other, with those on the sacred side of the boundary stones inscribed 'Sacred lands of Dionysos,' and those on the private land inscribed 'Boundary stones.' Similarly, on the boundary stone near the Fintias, we set up intermediate boundary stones: two on the road from the city and from Pandosia leading through the sacred lands, and two on the high ridges near the cheese-makers. All these, in alignment with those on the road through the gorge, with those on the sacred side inscribed 'Sacred lands of Dionysos,' and those on the private land inscribed 'Boundary stones,' at a distance of one hundred feet from each other. On the thirty-foot [path?] running through the sacred lands, on the upper side, two, thirty feet apart. And other intermediate boundary stones along the road past the woodland, two, thirty feet apart. And in the middle of the land on the thirty-foot [path?], four, thirty feet apart in one place, and twenty in another. On the boundary stone near the thirty-foot [path?], two, twenty feet apart. And another on the second boundary stone, twenty feet apart. Thus, all demarcated the portions, without inscription, for those who rented the sacred lands. The boundary stones mark the lands of Dionysos, from the upper boundary to the river Akiris, the ones near the heroön and near the Fintias. The number of boundary stones we set up: on the boundary stone near the heroön, seven, including the one on the side; on the thirty-foot [path?], eight, including the fourfold one; on the boundary stone near the thirty-foot [path?] and the next one, two on each; near the Fintias, seven, including the one near the canal and the ditch. Agreement concerning the sacred lands of Dionysos, during the magistracy of Aristion, month of Apellaios. The city and the polis-overseers [erected] the tripod for Philonymos, son of Zopyris; the spice box for Apollonios, son of Herakles; the shield for Dazimos, son of Pyrros; for Athena Polias. They inscribed them, the overseers who were chosen for the sacred lands of Athena in Koilai: Philonymos, son of Zopyris; Apollonios, son of Herakles; Dazimos, son of Pyrros, according to what they marked out, measured, finished, and divided. We measured the boundaries, as the Herakleians decreed in the assembly in Aliai, beginning from the boundary stone from Koinai, leading to the road, the thirty-foot [path?] leading to the sea. And from the boundary stone to the Boubētis, the seven gypes through the fields. From the Boubētis to the thirty-foot [path?], thirteen gypes. From the thirty-foot [path?] to the thirty-foot [path?] running through the trihemigypes, nine trihemigypes. Crossing the thirty-foot [path?], we measured towards the hekatostos, and we measured the tenth trihemigype. The trigypes were not completed as we found them done in ancient times, only a penthemigype remained from the two trigypes. Some had made the remaining land private; we restored it to Athena according to the ancient boundaries. From the hekatostos to the river Akiris, the land bordering the hundred-foot [path?] and the Herakleian road, some had made this entirely private. Some who had erected [boundaries] departed. We obtained judgments in thirty lawsuits against others, and having restored this land to the goddess according to the ancient [boundaries], we divided it. We placed boundary stones on each part, and made from the tenth trihemigype the first trigype, joined to the penthemigype, from the land we restored, so that its width was three gypes and its length from the hundred-foot [path?] to the Herakleian road. And they were measured: one hundred and thirty-eight schoinoi. Eight measurements. Three hundred and thirteen schoinoi of cultivated land, twenty-six feet. Four schoinoi of vineyard, ten measurements, three feet. This land was rented for the first five-year period at two hundred and sixty-nine medimnoi and two choinikes of grain. From this trigype, we measured to the hekatostos, a second trigype, its width along the boundaries, its length from the hundred-foot [path?] to the Herakleian road. And they were measured: one hundred and thirty-nine schoinoi; one hundred and twenty-three schoinoi of cultivated land, sixteen schoinoi of vineyard. This trigype was rented for six hundred and ninety-five medimnoi. Crossing the hekatostos, we made the first part near the hundred-foot [path?], where the vineyard is, and we marked out a common path from the hekatostos to the house, one hundred feet, and from the house to the vineyard, eight feet. And we measured from the hekatostos towards the Akiris, along the side division, from the common path leading to the hundred-foot [path?], and they were measured: fifty-nine and a half schoinoi. Fifty-one schoinoi of cultivated land, seven measurements, two feet. Eight schoinoi of vineyard, eight measurements. This was rented for four hundred and forty-six medimnoi, four choinikes. The second part, where the house is, its length from the hekatostos to the bank by the river, its width from the boundaries and the path eight feet long leading to the river, and to the boundaries. And they were measured: sixty-three schoinoi, twelve measurements. To this part, we assigned eight schoinoi of vineyard along the hundred-foot [path?], twenty-six feet and two [units]. And the whole part was seventy-two schoinoi, eight measurements, two feet. This was rented for six hundred and thirty-two medimnoi, and three choinikes. The third part, its length from the hekatostos to the bank by the river, its width from the boundaries of the second part to the boundaries. And they were measured: sixty-six and a half schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned seven schoinoi of vineyard along the hundred-foot [path?], seventeen measurements and two [units]. And the whole part was seventy-four schoinoi and two [units]. This was rented for six hundred and thirty medimnoi and two choinikes. The fourth part, its length from the hekatostos to the bank by the river, its width from the boundaries of the third part to the boundaries, and to the boundary stone marking the division of the lands, which we marked out from the hekatostos to the river, for common use by all who rented the sacred lands. And they were measured: sixty-eight schoinoi of cultivated land, thirteen measurements. To this part, we assigned fifteen schoinoi of vineyard along the hundred-foot [path?] that runs along the eight-foot path, and seven measurements. And the whole part was eighty-three schoinoi, twenty measurements. This was rented for six hundred and thirty medimnoi. From the boundary stone marking the lands, leading to the river, the hundred-foot [path?], we measured its length towards the Herakleian road, and its width from the hekatostos to the boundaries. And we left a path from the hekatostos to the house, one hundred feet. And this part was measured: sixty-two schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned six and a half schoinoi of vineyard along the hundred-foot [path?]. And the whole part was sixty-eight and a half schoinoi. This was rented for eight hundred and fifty-six medimnoi, and four choinikes. The second part, where the house is, from the boundary stone leading to the river, its length towards the Herakleian road, its width from the boundaries to the boundaries. And they were measured: fifty-nine and a half schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned six and a half schoinoi of vineyard from the hekatostos. And the whole part was sixty-six schoinoi. This was rented for four hundred and fifty-eight medimnoi, and fourteen and a half choinikes. The third part, from the hekatostos towards the vineyard, from the boundary stone leading to the river, its length towards the Herakleian road, its width from the boundaries to the boundaries. And they were measured: sixty-three and a half schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned six and a half schoinoi of vineyard from the hekatostos. And the whole part was seventy schoinoi. This was rented for three hundred and six medimnoi and four choinikes. The fourth part, from the hekatostos, its length from the boundary stone leading to the river, towards the path leading past the vineyard, its width from the boundaries to the boundaries. And they were measured: forty-eight schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned six and a half schoinoi of vineyard from the hekatostos. And the whole part was fifty-four and a half schoinoi. This was rented for two hundred and thirty-five medimnoi, and fifteen choinikes. The fifth part, from the hekatostos, its length from the boundary stone leading to the river, towards the path leading past the vineyard, its width from the boundaries to the island. And they were measured: sixty-four schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned seven schoinoi of vineyard from the hekatostos, seventeen measurements and two [units]. And the whole part was seventy-one schoinoi, seventeen measurements and two [units]. This was rented for five hundred and eighty medimnoi, and fifteen choinikes. The sixth part, the corner land, adjacent to the vineyard, along the Herakleian road and along the river. And they were measured: thirty schoinoi of cultivated land. To this part, we assigned eight and a half schoinoi of vineyard, which are adjacent to the plot. And the whole part was thirty-eight and a half schoinoi. This was rented for one medimnos.
EDCS-39100056.summary: A lengthy and detailed decree from an ancient Greek city (likely in Southern Italy or Sicily) concerning the surveying, division, lease, and management of sacred lands dedicated to Dionysos and Athena, including specifications for cultivation, boundaries, rents, and penalties.
